item.title: Hacker Uses AI Agent Platform Cairn to Breach Over 100 Websites
item.description:
Hacker Uses AI Agent Platform Cairn to Breach Over 100 Websites

A hacker breached more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that largely operated on their own, according to the AI security firm Norforge.

🔍 Overview

  • The attacks targeted companies in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japan.
  • Reuters identified victims that included John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.
  • Norforge described the attacker as the “most active” among the exposed Cairn instances it discovered.

🧩 How it works

  • Cairn is an open‑source AI platform that calls itself a “general‑purpose problem‑solving engine.”
  • Users define a start and end point for AI agents, which then document their progress as they move forward.
  • While designed for legitimate problem‑solving, Norforge notes that the same tool can be repurposed to orchestrate cyber‑attacks.
  • The hacker set “preferred intrusion tactics” in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, and successful breaches took about 23 hours.

⚙️ Key details

  • Scale: More than 100 compromised sites; over 20 exposed Cairn instances deemed “likely malicious.”
  • Human involvement: The AI agents carried out the attacks with little involvement from the human hacker.
  • Company responses:
    Company Reported impact
    John Deere No indication that sensitive information was accessed
    SharkNinja Breach affected a standalone site with product support information; threat contained
    Cummins Investigating a potential cyber‑attack on a website operated by a third‑party vendor
  • Norforge is working to have the malicious Cairn instances taken down.
  • Cairn’s creator, @le1xia0, stated the platform “was never a ‘hacking tool’” and that misuse is a human decision.

💡 Why it matters

  • The incidents illustrate how advanced AI tools can be weaponized to conduct large‑scale cyber‑attacks with minimal human direction.
  • As AI capabilities grow, the line between legitimate automation and malicious misuse becomes increasingly blurred, heightening concerns for cybersecurity professionals.

#AIagents #Cybersecurity #Cairn

Source: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents

item.title: SOCRadar Alerts Integration Brings External Threat Intel into Elastic Security
item.description:
SOCRadar Alerts Integration Brings External Threat Intel into Elastic Security

Your SOC runs on Elastic. Detections, logs, cases and dashboards all live in Kibana, and your analysts have built their muscle memory around it. Until now, external threat intelligence – alarms about the Surface, Deep and Dark Web, brand abuse or the external attack surface – arrived in a dedicated platform, were reviewed there, and then manually re‑keyed into the SIEM or case tool. The new SOCRadar Alerts integration (v0.1.0) eliminates that handoff.

🔎 Overview

  • The integration pulls SOCRadar alarms via the SOCRadar API on a configurable polling interval, with an initial historical look‑back to backfill recent alarms.
  • Each alarm arrives with severity, status, alarm type, sub‑type, affected asset, related entities and detailed information.
  • Alarm data is mapped to the Elastic Common Schema (ECS), so SOCRadar fields sit next to your other sources with consistent names.

🧩 How it works

  1. Polling – The integration queries the SOCRadar API on the schedule you set.
  2. Normalization – Incoming alarm fields are translated into ECS fields.
  3. Ingestion – Normalized alarm documents are stored in the same Elastic workspace used for internal telemetry.
  4. Visualization – A built‑in Kibana dashboard displays severity distribution, alarm categories, volume trends and recent incidents.
  5. Investigation – Analysts can pivot from a dashboard tile to the underlying alarm document, correlate it with endpoint or identity events, and open a case without leaving Kibana.

⚙️ Key details

  • Alarm attributes – Every alarm carries:
    • Severity
    • Status
    • Alarm type and sub‑type
    • Affected asset
    • Related entities
    • Detailed description
  • Analyst workflow – Search, filter and build rules on external alarms exactly as on internal telemetry; prioritize by severity across both.
  • Time saved – No manual copy‑paste between consoles; the external context that triggered the investigation is already in the case.
Attribute What it provides
Severity A severity level for prioritization
Status Current processing state of the alarm
Alarm type / sub‑type Classification of the finding
Affected asset The asset the alarm relates to
Related entities Additional objects linked to the alarm
Details Full description and context

🚀 Availability

  • The integration is listed in the Elastic integrations catalog. To enable it, open the catalog, search for SOCRadar, and add the SOCRadar Alerts integration with your SOCRadar API credentials and polling preferences.
  • If you are not yet a SOCRadar customer, or need help configuring the three integrations together, contact your SOCRadar customer success manager or request a demo.

💡 Why it matters

  • Unified workspace – External threat intelligence appears in the same Elastic Security workspace where analysts already work.
  • Reduced handoff – The costly manual step of re‑keying alarms is removed, eliminating bottlenecks caused by volume and lost context.
  • Actionable context – Each alarm includes the asset and related entities, so investigations start with concrete, validated information.
  • Continuous visibility – The built‑in Kibana dashboard gives immediate insight into spikes, such as a high‑severity “New Digital Asset Discovery” followed by an “Impersonating Domain” alarm, enabling rapid response.

#SOCRadar #ElasticSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #SIEM #ECS

Source: SOCRadar Alarms in Elastic | Investigate Threats Faster

item.title: AI Accelerates Vulnerability Disclosure and Exploitation, GTIG Finds
item.description:
AI Accelerates Vulnerability Disclosure and Exploitation, GTIG Finds

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) examined vulnerability disclosure and exploitation statistics to evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the vulnerability threat landscape.

🔍 Overview

  • The analysis covers January 1 2025 through August 31 2026.
  • GTIG uses its own Vulnerability Risk Ratings (not CVSS) and tracks exploitation consequences and in‑the‑wild exploitation.
  • AI‑assisted discovery produces proportionally fewer Low‑Risk findings, more Moderate‑Risk findings, and more Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

📈 Disclosure Growth

  • Vulnerability disclosures doubled:
    • 5,045 disclosed in January 2026.
    • 10,477 disclosed in July 2026.
    • 10,740 disclosed in August 2026 (peak).
  • High‑Risk disclosures surged 167 %:
    • 131 in January 2026 → 350 in August 2026 (3 % of all disclosures).
  • Baseline High‑Risk disclosures more than doubled across the broader software ecosystem:
    • ~65 /month in mid‑2025 → ~135 /month in mid‑2026.
  • Specific spikes:
    • 75 High‑Risk flaws added in April‑May 2026 from mass research on consumer router firmware.
    • 128 High‑Risk vulnerabilities in August 2026 from Oracle’s quarterly Critical Patch Update and Linux kernel network driver advisories (≈ 37 % of August High‑Risk total).
Month High‑Risk Disclosures
Jan 2026 131
Aug 2026 350

⚙️ Exploitation Trends

  • Average monthly exploited vulnerabilities rose from 10.5 (2025) to 18 (Jan‑Aug 2026).
  • Zero‑day exploitation increased from an average of 8 per month (2025) to 11 per month (Jan‑Aug 2026).
  • From Jan‑Aug 2026, GTIG recorded 141 distinct vulnerabilities that were both disclosed and exploited, surpassing the total of 127 for the entire year 2025.
  • Only 0.23 % of all disclosed vulnerabilities in 2026 (≈ 1 in 431) were ever observed in active exploitation.
  • Monthly exploitation counts can be influenced by vendor disclosure cycles and threat‑actor campaign spikes.

🛡️ Risk Implications

  • AI‑driven discovery is shifting the risk profile toward more Moderate‑Risk and RCE‑capable flaws.
  • High‑Risk vulnerabilities remain a small proportion of total disclosures but are growing rapidly.
  • Automated CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) assignment policies across open‑source ecosystems can inflate baseline figures.
  • Linux‑Kernel‑only descriptions generated ~5,000 CVEs (Jan‑Aug 2026) with zero observed in‑the‑wild zero‑day exploitation.

🚀 Recommendations

  • Organizations should move from unprioritized mass‑patching to threat‑intelligence‑driven triage.
  • Combine targeted edge‑defense with automated, agentic remediation to manage the faster discovery and exploitation velocity.
  • Monitor vendor disclosure cycles and threat‑actor activity to better anticipate exploitation spikes.

📅 Outlook

  • GTIG expects vulnerability discovery and exploitation to continue growing in the short to medium term.
  • Ongoing analysis will focus on growth velocity and emerging threat vectors across the AI/LLM operational stack.

#AI #VulnerabilityManagement #ThreatIntelligence #Cybersecurity

Source: Vulnerability Discovery and Exploitation Trends in the AI Era | Google Cloud Blog
